They were, from the seventh class: Cammerer, proveteranus, son of a court physician; Duttenhofer, veteranus primus, son of a game dealer, specialissimus; Vischer, novitius primus, son of a revenue-office secretary; [p. 432] from the sixth class: Boger, veteranus primus, son of a lieutenant-colonel; Hegel, novitius primus.

Man stellte uns weiter nichts vor, als daß man uns ernstlich ermahnte, unsere Cameraden zu warnen, sich nicht in elende liederliche Spielund andere Gesellschaften einzulassen. Es hat sich nämlich eine Gesellschaft von jungen Leuten männlichen Geschlechts von 16-17, weiblichen von 11-12 Jahren gezeigt. Sie ist unter dem Namen Doggengesellschaft, Lappländer u. s. w. bekannt. Die Herren führen da die Jungfern spazieren und verderben sich und die Zeit heilloser Weise.

Nothing further was put to us than that we were earnestly admonished to warn our comrades not to get involved in wretched, dissolute gambling and other societies. For a society of young people has come to light, males of 16–17, females of 11–12 years. It is known under the name of the Doggengesellschaft [Mastiff Society], Laplanders, etc. The gentlemen take the young ladies out walking there and ruin themselves and their time in a wretched way.

Dienstag den 28. Juni. Ich machte die Bemerkung, was für verschiedene Eindrücke einerlei Gegenstände auf verschiedene Personen machen können. Man erzählte nämlich, eine bekannte Frau sei glücklich niedergekommen. Mein Vater, als ein ehemaliger Ehemann, freute sich herzlich darüber. I. B. als eine erwachsene Weibsperson, die dergleichen Vorfällen schon beigewohnt hatte, noch mehr und sagte dabei, es sei doch keine größere Freude, als wenn eine Frau eine glückliche Niederkunft habe. Aber zu gleicher Zeit wurde ein schönes Pferd vorbeigeritten. B. und ich standen an den Fenstern. B., ohngefähr 21 Jahr alt, ein Mannsbild, fragte gleich, wem es gehöre, während man jene fröhliche Nachricht brachte, die er mehr mit Gleichgültigkeit hörte. Ich sprang zu ihm, nicht sonderlich durch die glückliche Niederkunft gerührt, und gab ihm Beifall, daß das ein recht schönes Pferd fei. Da ich Kirschen mit vielem Appetit aß und mich herrlich erlabte und glücklich schäßte, sah Iemand anders, freilich älter als ich, mit Gleichgültigkeit zu und sagte: in der Jugend glaube man, man könne unmöglich an einem Kirschweib vorbeigehen, ohne daß einem (wie wir Schwaben sagen) das Maul darnach wässere; in älteren Jahren aber könne man fast einen Frühling vorbeirollen lassen, ohne eben so darnach zu schmachten. Ich dachte hierbei den für mich ziemlich leidigen, aber doch allerweisesten Saz: daß man in der Jugend, wo man aus unhaltbarer Begierde gewiß seine Gesundheit in schlechte Umstände versehen würde, nicht so viel essen könne, im Alter nicht möge.

Tuesday, the 28th of June. I made the remark what different impressions one and the same object can make on different persons. Namely, it was told that a woman of my acquaintance had happily been delivered. My father, as an erstwhile husband, was heartily pleased at it; J. B., as a grown woman who had already attended such events, even more, and said besides that there is no greater joy than when a woman has a happy delivery. But at the same time a fine horse was ridden past. B. and I stood at the windows. B., about 21 years old, a fellow, asked at once whose it was, while that joyful news was being brought, which he heard rather with indifference. I sprang to him, not particularly moved by the happy delivery, and gave him my approval that it was a really fine horse. — As I was eating cherries with much appetite and delighting myself splendidly and counting myself happy, someone else, admittedly older than I, looked on with indifference and said: in youth one believes one could not possibly pass a cherry-woman without one’s (as we Swabians say) mouth watering for them; in older years, however, one can almost let a whole spring roll past without longing for it likewise. I thought thereupon the for me rather painful, but yet wisest saying: that in youth, when from irrepressible craving one would surely put one’s health into bad circumstances, one cannot eat so much, in old age one does not care to.

Mittwoch den 29. Juni. Ei, Ei! Schlimme Nachrichten von Ho- = henheim. Diese Bauern, das sind verwünschte Leute, habendem Herzog alle Fenster im Schloß zu Scharnhausen eingeworfen. Es war heut ein Feiertag. Ich ging aber nicht in die Kirch, sondern mit Duttenhofer und Autenrieth in den Bopserwald spazieren.

Wednesday, the 29th of June. Dear me, dear me! Bad news from Hohenheim. These peasants, they are accursed people, have smashed all the windows of the Duke’s castle at Scharnhausen. — It was a holiday today. But I did not go to church, but went walking in the Bopserwald with Duttenhofer and Autenrieth.

p. 433

Donnerstag den 30. Juni. Es war heut eine schwülige Hize und hatte das Anscheinen, als werd ' es ein Wetter geben, allein es verzog [p. 433] sich. - Ich spielte heute auch wiederum einmal mein beliebtes Schachspiel und ob ich gleich ein schlechter Spieler bin, so gewann ich es doch beidemal. Ich spiele nie nach einem Plan, wie es eigentlich geschehen sollte, sondern im Anfang nur auf's Gerathewohl, welches aber ein gro- Her Fehler ist. Das weitere Spielen und die Lage der Steine müssen alsdann den Plan bestimmen, nach dem ich weiter spielen werde. Ich will mich aber nächstens befleißen, diesen allemal gleich im Anfang zu machen und das ganze Spiel hindurch zu verfolgen. Ich sagte nur in fugam vacui so viel vom Schachspiel, damit doch der lekte Tag dieses Monats nicht leer bliebe.

Thursday, the 30th of June. There was a sultry heat today and it had the appearance as if there would be a thunderstorm, but it cleared away [p. 433] — I also played once again today my favorite chess, and although I am a poor player, I nevertheless won it both times. I never play according to a plan, as should actually be done, but at the beginning only at random, which however is a great fault. The further playing and the position of the pieces must then determine the plan according to which I shall play on. But I will endeavor next time to make this one each time right at the beginning and to follow it through the whole game. — I said so much about chess only in fugam vacui [to flee a void], so that the last day of this month might not remain empty.

Freitags den 1. Juli. Schon lange besann ich mich, was eine pragmatische Geschichte sei. Ich habe heut ' eine obgleich ziemlich dunkle und einseitige Idee davon erhalten. Eine pragmatische Geschichte ist, glaub ' ich, wenn man nicht blos Facta erzählt, sondern auch den Charakter eines berühmten Mannes, einer ganzen Nation, ihre Sitten, Gebräuche, Religion und die verschiedenen Veränderungen und Abweichungen dieser Stücke von andern Völkern entwickelt; dem Zerfall und dem Emporsteigen großer Reiche nachspürt; zeigt, was diese oder jene Begebenheit oder Staatsveränderung für die Verfassung der Nation, für ihren Charakter u. s. f. für Folgen gehabt u. dgl. m.

Friday, the 1st of July. For a long time I had been pondering what a pragmatic history is. Today I have obtained an idea of it, though a rather obscure and one-sided one. A pragmatic history is, I believe, when one does not merely narrate facts, but also develops the character of a famous man, of a whole nation, its customs, usages, religion and the various changes and deviations of these items from other peoples; traces the decline and the rise of great empires; shows what this or that event or change of state has had for consequences for the constitution of the nation, for its character, etc., and the like.

Samstag den 2. Juli. Warum hat Sokrates vor seinem Ende dem Aeskulapius einen Hahn opfern lassen? fragte Herr Prof. Offerdinger in einem Hebdomadario. Nach Anführung verschiedener Meinungen sagte er: er halte dafür, Sokrates seie durch die Wirkung des Giftes sich seiner nimmer bewußt gewesen. Ich halte neben dieser Ursach auch davor, er habe gedacht, weil es Sitte sei, wolle er durch Unterlassung dieser geringen Gabe den Pöbel nicht vollends vor den Kopf stoßen.

Saturday, the 2nd of July. Why did Socrates have a cock sacrificed to Aesculapius before his end? asked Professor Offerdinger in a Hebdomadarium [weekly exercise]. After citing various opinions he said: he held that Socrates, through the effect of the poison, was no longer conscious of himself. I hold, besides this cause, also that he thought, since it was the custom, he did not wish, by omitting this slight gift, to affront the rabble altogether.

Sonntag den 3. Juli. Auf dem Rückweg eines Spaziergangs stellten wir, besonders ich (daß doch die Eigenliebe gleich ins Spiel muß!), den Saz auf: „jedes Gute hat seine böse Seite (oft minder, oft mehr, nach Verhältniß des Guten) und wendeten diesen Saz bei jedem Tritt an. R., der auch mit war, ging um ein anderes Eck, als wir. Es war weiter. Wie wir ihn gegen uns kommen sahen, warteten wir. Nun sagte einer: was dieses Warten und Aufhalten im Weg an sich Gutes habe, sehe er nicht ein. Wir antworteten: wenn wir fortgeloffenwären, hätte einer fallen oder einen nicht guten Gedanken haben können. Recht stoisch!

Sunday, the 3rd of July. On the way back from a walk we set up, I especially (that self-love must come into play at once!), the proposition: “every good has its bad side (often less, often more, in proportion to the good) and applied this proposition at every step. R., who was also along, went around another corner than we. It was farther. As we saw him come toward us, we waited. Now one said: what good this waiting and stopping on the way has in itself, he did not see. We answered: if we had run on, one of us might have fallen or had a not good thought. — Quite stoic!

p. 434

Montag den 4. Juli. Auf dem Spaziergang examinirte mich Herr Prof. Cloß wegen unterschiedlicher Materien, besonders wegen dem Lauf 28 [p. 434] der Sonne oder vielmehr der Neigung der Erde, wodurch die Jahreszeiten entstehen. Unter Anderem machte ich die Frage: warum es im Juli und August heißer sei, als im Juni, wo doch die Sonne sich uns am meisten nähere? Daß die Hize in unserer Atmosphäre durch die Abprallung der Sonnenstrahlen entstehe, ist bekannt. Herr Prof. Cloß ertheilten mir nun folgende Erklärung: Im Juni und bälder erweckt und irritirt die Sonne gleichsam durch ihre Taction und Entzündung die Feuertheile nahe auf der Oberfläche der Erde. Diese irritiren nun wieder die neben sich liegenden und gehen so gleichsam in einer Rette fort bis in den Mittelpunct der Erde. Im Juli und August mögen nun die meisten irritirt sein. In diesen Monaten wird also die größte Hize aus der Erde in die Atmosphäre zurückgeworfen und es ist also am heißesten.

Monday, the 4th of July. On the walk Professor Cloß examined me on various subjects, especially on the course of [p. 434] the sun or rather the inclination of the earth, whereby the seasons arise. Among other things I put the question: why it is hotter in July and August than in June, when the sun is yet nearest to us? That the heat in our atmosphere arises through the rebounding of the sun’s rays is known. Professor Cloß gave me the following explanation: In June and sooner the sun, as it were, excites and irritates, through its taction and ignition, the fire-particles near the surface of the earth. These now in turn irritate those lying beside them and so go on, as it were, in a chain to the center of the earth. In July and August most of them may now be irritated. In these months, then, the greatest heat is thrown back from the earth into the atmosphere and it is therefore hottest.

Dienstag den 5. Juli. Ich kaufte aus der Bibliothek des seligen Herrn Präceptor Löffler, meines treuesten Lehrers und Führers, folgende Bücher: 1. Griechische: Aristoteles de moribus; Demosthenis oratio de corona; Isocratis opera omnia; 2. Lateinische: a. prosaische: Ciceronis opera philosophica; A. Gellii noctes Atticae; Vellejus Paterculus; Diodorus Siculus; b. poetische: Plautus; Catullus, Tibullus, Propertius; Gallus, Claudianus und Ausonius; Hieronymus Vida; Virgilius Christianus; Sannazarius.

Tuesday, the 5th of July. I bought from the library of the late Preceptor Löffler, my most faithful teacher and guide, the following books: 1. Greek: Aristoteles de moribus [Aristotle on morals]; Demosthenis oratio de corona [Demosthenes’ oration on the crown]; Isocratis opera omnia [the complete works of Isocrates]; 2. Latin: a. prose: Ciceronis opera philosophica [Cicero’s philosophical works]; A. Gellii noctes Atticae [Aulus Gellius’s Attic Nights]; Vellejus Paterculus; Diodorus Siculus; b. poetic: Plautus; Catullus, Tibullus, Propertius; Gallus, Claudianus and Ausonius; Hieronymus Vida; Virgilius Christianus; Sannazarius.

Mittwoch den 6. Juli. Herr Präceptor Löffler war einer meiner verehrungswürdigsten Lehrer, besonders im untern Gymnasio darf ich ihn kecklich fast den vorzüglichsten nennen.

Wednesday, the 6th of July. Preceptor Löffler was one of my most venerable teachers; especially in the lower Gymnasium I may boldly call him almost the most excellent.

Donnerstag den 7. Juli. Er war der rechtschaffenste und unpartheiischste Mann. Seinen Schülern, sich und der Welt zu nügen, war seine Hauptsorge. Er dachte nicht so niedrig, wie Andere, welche glauben, jezt haben sie ihr Brod und dürfen nicht weiter studiren, wenn sie nur den ewigen alle Jahr erneueten Classenschlendrian fortmachen können. Nein, so dachte der Selige nicht. Er kannte den Werth der Wissenschaften und den Trost, den sie einem bei verschiedenen Zufällen gereichen. Wie oft und wie zufrieden und heiter saß er bei mir in jenem geliebten Stübchen und ich bei ihm! - Wenige kannten seine Verdienste. Ein großes Unglück war es für den Mann, daß er so ganz unter seiner Sphäre arbeiten mußte. Und nun ist er auch entschlafen! Aberewig werde ich sein Andenken unverrückt in meinem Herzen tragen. Dieß muß ich doch hinzufügen, daß er mir 8 Bände von Shakespeares Schauspielen schon 1778 zum Geschenk machte.

Thursday, the 7th of July. He was the most upright and impartial man. His chief concern was to be useful to his pupils, to himself and to the world. He did not think so basely as others who believe: now they have their bread and need study no further, if only they can keep up the eternal class routine renewed every year. No, the blessed man did not think so. He knew the worth of the sciences and the comfort which they afford one in various mishaps. How often and how contentedly and cheerfully he sat with me in that beloved little room, and I with him! — Few knew his merits. It was a great misfortune for the man that he had to work so entirely beneath his sphere. And now he too has fallen asleep! But forever shall I bear his memory unremoved in my heart. — This I must still add, that he made me a present of 8 volumes of Shakespeare’s plays as early as 1778.

p. 435

Freitag den 8. Juli. Us einen allgemeinen Zug habe ich bei dem [p. 435] Charakter des weiblichen Geschlechts (manche Männer sind gewiß auch nicht frei davon) die gänzliche Uebertretung der Verse des Horaz angetroffen, welche so lauten:

Friday, the 8th of July. As a general trait I have in the [p. 435] character of the female sex (some men too are certainly not free from it) found the complete violation of the verses of Horace, which read thus:

Sperat in festis, metuit secundis Alteram sortem bene praeparatum Pectus.

[Latin] In adversity it hopes, in prosperity it fears / A change of lot, the well-prepared / Heart.

Samstag den 9. Juli. Hat je der Aberglaube ein schreckliches, unter aller Menschenvernunft dummes Abenteuer ausgebrütet, so ist es gewiß das sogenannte Muthesheer (muthiges Heer). Am vergangenen Sonntag Nachts um 1 oder 2 Uhr haben viele Leute es zu sehen behauptet, sogar, pudendum dictu, Leute von denen man mehr Aufklärung erwartet und die in öffentlichen Aemtern stehen. Dieses alte Weib will einen feurigen Wagen mit Menschen gesehen haben, jenes wieder was Anderes. Gemeiniglich sagt man, es seie der Teufel in einem feurigen Wagen. Voran fliege ein Engel Gottes und rufe Iedermann zu: aus dem Wege, das muthige Heer kommt! Wer diesem göttlichen Ruf nicht folge, werde vom Herrn Teufel in seine Residenz geschleift.

Saturday, the 9th of July. If ever superstition has hatched a terrible adventure, stupid beneath all human reason, it is certainly the so-called Muthesheer (Valiant Host). Last Sunday night at 1 or 2 o’clock many people claimed to have seen it, even, pudendum dictu [shameful to say], people from whom one expects more enlightenment and who hold public offices. This old woman claims to have seen a fiery wagon with human beings, that one something else again. Commonly it is said that it is the devil in a fiery wagon. An angel of God flies ahead and calls to everyone: out of the way, the Valiant Host is coming! Whoever does not obey this divine call is dragged off by Herr Devil into his residence.

Sonntag den 10. Juli. Doch auf das muthige Heer zu kommen, so sind mir verschiedene Personen genannt worden, die es gesehen oder gehört haben (es ist nämlich ein abscheuliches Gerassel). Einige Tage hernach klärte es sich auf, daß eso Schande, Schande! - Kutschen waren! Herr v. Türkheim gab nämlich ein Concert, das sehr zahlreich war und bis um 1 oder 2 Uhr dauerte. Um nun die Gäste nicht in der Finsterniß heimtappen zu lassen, ließ er sie mit Kutschen und Fackeln heimführen. Und das war dies muthige Heer. Ha, ha, ha! O tempora, o mores! Geschehen Anno 1785. O, o!

Sunday, the 10th of July. But to come back to the Valiant Host, various persons have been named to me who have seen or heard it (it is namely an abominable clatter). Some days afterward it turned out that it — oh shame, shame! — was coaches! Herr von Türkheim namely gave a concert, which was very well attended and lasted till 1 or 2 o’clock. In order then not to let the guests grope home in the darkness, he had them taken home with coaches and torches. And that was this Valiant Host. Ha, ha, ha! O tempora, o mores! [O the times, O the customs!] Happened in the year 1785. Oh, oh!

Montag den 11. Juli. Bei diesem Vorfall trug sich noch folgende Anekdote zu. Bürgersleute kamen auf die Hauptwacht und erzählten jenen Vorgang und baten zugleich den commandirenden Offizier, er möchte Acht geben lassen, ob denn das muthige Heer wiederkäme? Der Lieutenant befahl darauf, Acht zu geben. Der Soldat, der vielleicht noch nichts davon gehört hatte, fragte: wenn es kommt, befehlen Ew. Gnaden, der Herr Lieutenant, daß ich es anhalten soll? - Ja, ja, sagte der Lieutenant, halt's nur an. Es blieb aber aus.

Monday, the 11th of July. On this occasion the following anecdote also occurred. Townspeople came to the main guard and told of that incident and at the same time asked the commanding officer to have a watch kept whether the Valiant Host would come again. The lieutenant thereupon ordered a watch to be kept. The soldier, who perhaps had not yet heard anything of it, asked: if it comes, does Your Honor, Lieutenant, command that I should halt it? — Yes, yes, said the lieutenant, just halt it. — But it stayed away.

p. 436

Dienstag den 12. Juli. Eine ähnliche Geschichte ereignete sich neulich. Vier Frauenzimmer fuhren vom Chausseehaus auf der Ludwigsburgerstraße hieher, wobei man am Galgen vorbeikommt. Es war um 12 Uhr Nachts. Beim Chausseehäuslein sei nun ein reitender Postknecht ohne Kopf zu ihnen gekommen und immer bald neben, bald vor, bald 28 * [p. 436] hinter der Kutsche mit ihnen geritten. Der Kutscher wollte ausweichen, allein der Postknecht folgte immer, bis er endlich am Thor verschwand. Das beruhete doch auf der Aussage von 5 oder 6 Personen. Gr etliche Tage nachher erklärte ein Offizier, daß er gerade an demselben Ort und zu derselben Zeit zu einer Kutsche gekommen und mitgeritten sei, habe aber nicht durch dies Thor hinein mögen, sei also von ihnen hinweg und einen andern Weg geritten. Er sagte dabei, er habe nicht begreifen können, warum ihm der Kutscher immer habe ausweichen wollen.

Tuesday, the 12th of July. A similar story happened recently. Four women were driving from the turnpike house on the Ludwigsburg road to here, whereby one passes the gallows. It was at 12 o’clock at night. At the little turnpike house a mounted post-boy without a head had now come to them and kept riding with them, now beside, now before, now [p. 436] behind the coach. The coachman wanted to evade him, but the post-boy always followed, until at last he vanished at the gate. That, however, rested on the testimony of 5 or 6 persons. — Only some days afterward an officer declared that he had come at just the same place and at the same time upon a coach and ridden along with it, but had not wanted to go in through this gate, and had therefore ridden away from them by another way. He said at the same time that he had not been able to understand why the coachman had always wanted to evade him.

Mittwoch den 13. Juli. Ich war heute das erstemal auf der herzoglichen Bibliothek. Alle Mittwoch und Samstag von 2-5 steht es einem Jeden frei, sie zu besuchen. In einem großen Zimmer, wo man sich aufhält, steht eine lange Tafel mit Feder und Papier. Das Buch, das man begehrt, schreibt man nächst dem Namen auf einem Papier und giebt es dem Bedienten, der einem dann das Buch überbringt. Ich forderte, weil andere Bücher nicht da waren, Batteux Einleitung in die schönen Wissenschaften und las das Stück von der Epopee.

Wednesday, the 13th of July. I was today for the first time in the ducal library. Every Wednesday and Saturday from 2–5 it is open to everyone to visit it. In a large room where one waits there stands a long table with pen and paper. The book one wants one writes, next to one’s name, on a slip of paper and gives it to the attendant, who then brings the book over. I asked, because other books were not there, for Batteux’s Introduction to the Belles Lettres and read the section on the epopee.

Donnerstag den 14. Juli. Die Herren Professoren Abel und Hopf beehrten unsere Gesellschaft vorgestern mit einem Besuch. Wir gingen mit ihnen spazieren, wo sie uns besonders von Wien unterhielten.

Thursday, the 14th of July. Professors Abel and Hopf honored our society the day before yesterday with a visit. We went walking with them, where they entertained us especially about Vienna.

Freitag den 15. Juli. Ich ging mit Herrn Prof. Cloß spazieren. Wir lasen in Mendelssohn's Phädon, nur so gleichsam die Vorbereitung oder Einleitung, nämlich den Charakter des Sokrates. Anytus, Melitus und Krito waren die drei Scheusale, die ihm den Tod von dem furchtsamen Senat und dem tollköpfigen Pöbel auswirkten.

Friday, the 15th of July. I went walking with Professor Cloß. We read in Mendelssohn’s Phaedo, only as it were the preparation or introduction, namely the character of Socrates. Anytus, Melitus and Crito were the three monsters who procured his death from the timorous senate and the hotheaded rabble.

Samstag den 16. Juli. Es starb heute Herr Stadtschreiber Kläpflel, da man ihn schon auf dem Rückweg zur Genesung glaubte.

Saturday, the 16th of July. Town Clerk Kläpfel died today, when one already believed him on the way back to recovery.

Dienstag den 19. Juli. Eben so starb heute Herr Regierungsrath und Geheime Cabinets = Secretair Schmidlin an einem Schlage, wie er den Löffel zum Essen in die Hand nehmen wollte. Leypold, ein guter Freund von mir, ist einer seiner Enkel.

Tuesday, the 19th of July. Likewise Government Councillor and Privy Cabinet Secretary Schmidlin died today of a stroke, as he was about to take the spoon in hand to eat. Leypold, a good friend of mine, is one of his grandsons.

Mittwoch den 20. Juli. Ich war heute wieder auf der Bibliothek und bat um Dusch's Briefe zur Bildung des Geschmacks, allein entweder waren sie nicht da oder man konnte sie nicht finden. Ich erhielt sie nicht, las also wieder im Rammler. Ich spielte auch mit Herrn Riedrer zweimal Schach, worin ich es allemal gewann.

Wednesday, the 20th of July. I was today again at the library and asked for Dusch’s Letters on the Formation of Taste, but either they were not there or they could not be found. I did not get them, and so read again in the Rammler. — I also played chess twice with Herr Riedrer, in which I won every time.

p. 437

Donnerstag den 21. Iuli. Ich ging mit Herrn Cloß spazieren. Wie wir über den Graben gingen, läutete man die große Glocke zum Begräbniß des Herrn Reg. R. Schmidlin's. Zugleich sing man an, mit [p. 437] 2 Posaunen von dem Stadtthurm moles propinqua nubibus arduis! Trauer zu blasen. Der dumpfe, feierliche, langsame Ton der Glocke und der traurige Schall der Posaunen machten einen solch erhabenen Eindruck auf mich, den ich nicht beschreiben kann, indem ich zugleich: manchmal von weitem die Kutschen sah und an die Klagen der Hinterlassenen dachte.

Thursday, the 21st of July. I went walking with Herr Cloß. As we were crossing the moat, the great bell was being tolled for the burial of Government Councillor Schmidlin. At the same time they began with [p. 437] trombones from the town tower — moles propinqua nubibus arduis [a mass rising near the lofty clouds] — to blow a dirge. The dull, solemn, slow tone of the bell and the sad sound of the trombones made such a sublime impression on me, which I cannot describe, as I at the same time sometimes saw the coaches from afar and thought of the laments of the bereaved.

Freitag den 22. Juli. Ich ging mit Herrn Prof. Cloß wieder spazieren; er examinirte mich in den regulären und irregulären Körpern.

Friday, the 22nd of July. I went walking again with Professor Cloß; he examined me on the regular and irregular solids.

Die Lehre von denselben beschäftigt Hegel in seinem Tagebuch ausführlich bis zum 25. Juli. Am 29. tritt eine neue Epoche in dasselbe mit dem Lateinschreiben ein.

The doctrine of these occupies Hegel at length in his diary up to 25 July. On the 29th a new epoch enters it, with writing in Latin.

Freitag den 29. Iuli. Exercendi styli et roboris acquirendi causa non alienum videtur, notam quandam historiam latino idiomate conscribere. Constitutum igitur habeo, res Romanas brevi percurrere et primoribus saltim labiis degustare. Urbem conditam a Romulo, primo Romulidum rege, a principio reges habuerunt. Quorum novissimo superbiente populique iura imminuente, aliam maluerunt cives formam dominationis etc.

Friday, the 29th of July. [Latin] For the sake of exercising style and acquiring strength it seems not inappropriate to write down a certain well-known story in the Latin idiom. I have therefore resolved to run briefly through Roman affairs and to taste them, at least with the tips of my lips. The city, founded by Romulus, the first king of the Romulidae, had kings from the beginning. When the last of them grew arrogant and curtailed the rights of the people, the citizens preferred another form of government, etc.

Samstag den 30. Juli. Saepenumero equidem mirari soleo, mirandas rerum fortunas. Ciceronis officia et Dialogi in manibus sunt, 1582 typis impressi. Duorum annorum spatio non praeterlapso libri vetustatem, quam pertulerat, admiratus, mecum reputavi: ducentos annos revolutos esse, cum liber iste typis imprimeretur. Reputans igitur mecum tot manus, quae in conficienda libri impressione sedulo detentae sunt, hominesque, quorum consiliis illae rectae, nunc oblivione posteritatis premi, nescio, quid dicam? Doluissent sane homines illi incolumes, si compertum habuissent, post mortem descensuram ex animis hominum memoriam sui, memoriam virtutum, memoriam bene factorum. Jam quidem alia plane sentire hos homines non dubito.

Saturday, the 30th of July. [Latin] I am indeed often wont to wonder at the wonderful fortunes of things. The Offices of Cicero and the Dialogues are in my hands, printed in 1582. Before a space of two years had elapsed, marveling at the age of the book, which it had endured, I reckoned with myself that two hundred years had rolled by since that book was printed. Reflecting then with myself that so many hands, which were diligently kept busy in producing the printing of the book, and the men by whose counsels those hands were directed, are now pressed down by the oblivion of posterity, I know not what I should say? Those men, had they remained alive, would surely have grieved, if they had learned that after death the memory of themselves, the memory of their virtues, the memory of their good deeds would fall away from the minds of men. Now, however, I do not doubt that these men feel quite otherwise.

Sonntag den 31. Juli. Deficiente alia quadam materia, Adrasti calamitates paucis enarrabo. Adrastus, Phrygiae regis filius, etc.

Sunday, the 31st of July. [Latin] For lack of any other material, I shall narrate in a few words the calamities of Adrastus. Adrastus, son of the king of Phrygia, etc.

p. 438

Montag den 1. August. De Graecae linguae difficultate saepius mecum reputans has fere reperi causas. Graeci, coaevorum facile doctissimi, politissimi, fortissimi, barbarorum literas parce omnino didicerunt; cum barbaris gentibus, quas ut rudes contemserunt, parva erat illis consuetudo. Oppressorum populorum linguas victores vel deleverunt [p. 438] suamque intulerunt, vel inter plebem solam serpere passi sunt. Qua in linguarum ruditate paternam magis excoluerunt, ampliaverunt. Qua ex re maxima Graecarum literarum orta est opulentia, quae plurimas peregrino parit difficultates.

Monday, the 1st of August. [Latin] Reflecting rather often with myself on the difficulty of the Greek language, I have found, roughly, these causes. The Greeks, easily the most learned, the most polished, the bravest of their contemporaries, learned the letters of the barbarians only sparingly; with barbarian peoples, whom as rude they despised, they had little intercourse. The languages of oppressed peoples the victors either destroyed [p. 438] [Latin] and brought in their own, or allowed them to creep about only among the common people. In this rudeness of languages they cultivated and enlarged their native tongue all the more. From this arose the very great wealth of Greek letters, which causes the foreigner a great many difficulties.

Mittwoch den 3. August. Magnum cumulum addiderunt formae civitatum illimitata libertate. Summa plerumque rerum plebi subjecta, si quis valere aliquid aut efficere studuit, nihil potius esse debuit, quam auram popularem captare et sic consilia perficere. Sagaciorem non diu fugit, ad omnia adduci plebem oris eloquentia. Eo diligentius huic incubuerunt et linguam ad elegantiam et venustatem con-

Wednesday, the 3rd of August. [Latin] The unlimited liberty of the form of their states added a great heap. Since supreme power was for the most part subject to the people, whoever strove to have any weight or to accomplish anything had to do nothing rather than court popular favor, and so carry through his plans. It did not long escape the more sagacious that the people could be led to anything by eloquence of speech. All the more diligently did they apply themselves to it, and shaped the language to elegance and charm.

formarunt. Donnerstag den 4. August. Accedit multitudo, elegantia et ornatus Particularum. Numerum vero Graecorum imitari nostro tempore sane non valemus, cum pessimarum vocum usu plane sit depravatus. Sonntag den 7. August. Primo interfui hodie divino Catholicorum cultui orationique sacrae, quam a Werkmeister concionatus est. Missa, quam vocant, nondum erat finita, cum venirem, quae quidem mihi, ut sano cuivis hominum, maxime displicuit. Hymno decantato, ipsa secuta est oratio, quae mihi ita placuit, ut saepius hanc concionem adire statuerim. Spectavit tota eo, ut rudibus rigideque duram vetustatem retinentibus mitiora, aliorum Christianorum, licet a suis doctrinis differentium amantiora conformaret ingenia. Non auditum ne unum quidem verbum, ex quo conspici potuisset flebilis illa Christia-

Thursday, the 4th of August. [Latin] To this is added the multitude, elegance and ornament of the particles. The rhythm of the Greeks, however, we are in our time certainly unable to imitate, since it has been utterly corrupted by the use of the worst words. Sunday, the 7th of August. [Latin] Today for the first time I attended the divine service of the Catholics and the sacred oration which Werkmeister preached. The Mass, as they call it, was not yet finished when I arrived; it displeased me exceedingly, as it would any sane man. After a hymn had been sung, the oration itself followed, which pleased me so much that I resolved to attend this preacher more often. Its whole aim was to make the minds of the uncultivated, who rigidly retain harsh antiquity, milder and more loving towards other Christians, even though these differ from their own doctrines. Not a single word was heard from which that lamentable discord of the Christians could have been discerned.

norum discordia. Montag den 8. August. Silentio non praetermittendum sane esse in hac factorum enarratione, in Collegio Rev. Dni. Prof. Clessii praestantissimas Livii historias sub DEI auspiciis nos hodie inchoasse. Libata est a summe rever. Professore Livii vita, de qua quidem pauca ad nos pervenerunt. Quae equidem didici, paucis commemorabo. Livius Patavinus sub Augusto floruit etc.

Monday, the 8th of August. [Latin] It must surely not be passed over in silence in this narration of events that today, under God’s auspices, we began the most excellent histories of Livy in the class of the Reverend Professor Cless. The most reverend professor touched on the life of Livy, of which indeed little has come down to us. What I learned I shall record in a few words. Livy of Padua flourished under Augustus, etc.

Sonntag den 21. August. Interfui hodie Catholicorum iterum sacris. Majer interpretatus est Catechismum, quae quidem expositio et venerabili interpretis eruditione et maxima perspicuitate mire mihi placuit. Ante meridiem recens cooptatus arcessitusque rei divinae minister publicam habuit de virtute orationem, cui quidem me non adfuisse valde poenituit.

Sunday, the 21st of August. [Latin] Today I again attended the sacred rites of the Catholics. Majer expounded the Catechism, and this exposition pleased me wonderfully both by the venerable learning of the expositor and by its very great perspicuity. Before noon a minister of divine things, recently co-opted and called, gave a public oration on virtue, and I greatly regretted not having been present at it.

p. 439

Montag den 22. August. Saepius et ego mecum ipse reputavi et libris etiam quae perpendantur digna reperi, quaenam sit vehementissima animi perturbatio, quae plurimas intulerit in homines, urbes, [p. 439] civitates, regna calamitates? Videamus igitur, quae effecerint honoris libido, auri, amor, superbia, invidia, desperatio, odium, ira et ultionis libido.

Monday, the 22nd of August. [Latin] I too have often reflected by myself, and have also found in books things worthy of being weighed, which is the most violent perturbation of the mind, the one that has brought the most calamities upon men, cities, [p. 439] states, kingdoms? Let us see, therefore, what the desire for honor, the love of gold, pride, envy, despair, hatred, anger and the desire for revenge have brought about.

Dienstag den 23. August. Procul dubio honoris libido publicas clades maximas attulit, sociata cum imperii cupidine. Quid Alexandrum M. Dario, a quo nunquam laesus fuit, funestissimum bellum ut inferret, impulit? Quid Timurem, Persiae regem, qui Asiam longe lateque victoribus Tartaris, victricibus armis immensa gloria peragravit? Quid tot praestantissimos Romanorum duces, quos referre immensi esset operis? Nonne haec commotio Academicis immisit funestissima certamina, quae duella vocant, quae tot florentium juvenum stamina, tot unica parentum solamina et gaudia dissecuerunt?

Tuesday, the 23rd of August. [Latin] Beyond doubt the desire for honor has brought the greatest public disasters, allied with the lust for dominion. What drove Alexander the Great to wage a most deadly war against Darius, by whom he had never been harmed? What Timur, king of Persia, who with Tartar victors, with victorious arms and immense glory ranged over Asia far and wide? What so many most distinguished leaders of the Romans, whom to enumerate would be a task of immense labor? Has not this commotion sent upon academic youth the most deadly contests, which they call duels, which have cut the threads of so many flourishing youths, so many only consolations and joys of parents?

Mittwoch den 24. August. Inter barbaras rudesque gentes virtutis non est alius impulsus praeter honorem et patriae, parentum, uxorum, liberorum amorem? Idem de majoribus nostris constat, devastasse illos immensa agrorum arvorumque spatia et inferis adjunxisse infinitum hominum numerum, ut nomen sibi per vicinitatem non solum, sed totam Germaniam acquirerent. Hactenus de honoris cupidine. Ad alia redeamus.

Wednesday, the 24th of August. [Latin] Among barbarous and rude peoples is there any other impulse of virtue besides honor and love of fatherland, parents, wives, children? The same is established concerning our ancestors, that they laid waste immense stretches of fields and farmlands and sent to the dead an infinite number of men, in order to acquire a name for themselves not only through their neighborhood but through all Germany. So far on the desire for honor. Let us return to other things.

Hier solgt im Tagebuch eine Unterbrechung bis zum December. Die Ursache erzählt Hegel selbst. Er hatte sich zu einem Examen bei bereits angegriffener Gesundheit angestrengt und bekam eine Geschwulst am Halse, welche ihm der Arzt Conspruch und der Chirurg Mohrstadt heilten.

Here there follows in the diary an interruption until December. Hegel himself relates the cause. He had exerted himself for an examination with his health already impaired and got a swelling on the neck, which the physician Conspruch and the surgeon Mohrstadt cured.

V. a. Id. Decb. Constitutum habeo, diarium hoc, et per examen nostrum Prid. Non. et ipsis Non. Septembr. habitum, et potissimum, qui me invasit, per morbum et gravem et diuturnum, longo temporis intervallo intermissum, jam resumere et pristina studia stylo exercendo renovare. Cujus igitur juvabit, temporis historiam brevi percurrere.

[Latin] The 5th day before the Ides of December. I have resolved to resume now this diary, interrupted for a long interval of time by the examination held by us on the day before the Nones and on the Nones of September themselves, and most of all by the illness, both grave and lasting, which seized me, and to renew my former studies by exercising my style. It will therefore be pleasing to run briefly through the history of that time.

p. 440

Aliquot ante examen diebus jam valetudine aliquantum fessus, tamen me non cohibui, quin illud examen, dissuadentibus et edoctoribus et aliis, adirem. Feliciter illo absoluto, domus nostrae limen ulterius egressus non sum. Vehementi morbo correptus, ereptus tamen medici diligentia et medicamentis mature adhibitis. Collo sinistra parte valde intumui, omni morbi peste et sanie illuc collecta. Diu multumque hoc inflatu discruciato arte Chirurgii Mohrstadtii Medicique Conspruchii laxamentum allatum, quorum quidem prior, dissecto tumore, vulnus duarum pollicis latitudinis inflixit, ut saniei cruorisque tetra copia [p. 440] emanaret paene per triduum, quod diligentia Chirurgii frequentique deligatione inter dies circiter triginta coaluit, a secto enim vulnere a. d. VI. Non. Oct. Gymnasium rursus pridie Calend. Novb. frequentavi.

Some days before the examination, already somewhat wearied by ill health, I nevertheless did not restrain myself from going to that examination, though my teachers and others dissuaded me. That having happily been completed, I did not go beyond the threshold of our house again. Seized by a violent illness, I was nevertheless rescued by the diligence of the physician and by medicines promptly applied. I swelled greatly in the neck on the left side, all the poison and corruption of the disease having collected there. After long and much torment from this swelling, relief was brought by the art of the surgeon Mohrstadt and the physician Conspruch, of whom the former, having cut open the tumor, inflicted a wound two thumb-widths wide, so that a foul abundance of pus and blood [p. 440] flowed out for almost three days; which, by the diligence of the surgeon and frequent bandaging, closed up within about thirty days; for from the cutting of the wound, on the 6th day before the Nones of October, I attended the Gymnasium again on the day before the Calends of November.

IV. Id. Debr. Quae dum mecum agebantur, multa alia extra me memoria digna contigerunt. Carissimus mihi amicus ablatus est a nobis Tubingam Theologiae consecraneus, puto J. F. Duttenhoferum. Mortuus est eodem temporis spatio celeberrimus ille, decus maximum patriae nostrae Moser, qui tot, quot perlegere humana non sufficit aetas, perscripsit libros, qui tot tamque variis (casibus) jactatus vitam egit. Mortuus est dignitate insignis rebusque aliis, quas hic referre alienum est, Hochsteter. Mortuus est denique ille et genere et opibus clarus de Herzberg.

[Latin] The 4th day before the Ides of December. While these things were being done with me, many other things worthy of memory happened apart from me. A most dear friend of mine was taken from us to Tübingen, one dedicated to theology, I think J. F. Duttenhofer. At the same span of time died that most celebrated man, the greatest ornament of our fatherland, Moser, who wrote so many books, as many as a human lifetime does not suffice to read through, who lived a life tossed about by so many and so various (chances). Died, distinguished in dignity and in other things which it is not fitting to relate here, Hochsteter. Died finally that man, illustrious in birth and wealth, de Herzberg.

III. Id. Debr. Aucta etiam est interea bibliothecula mea libris aliquot. Emi enim jam dudum: 1. Livium, ex meo aerario sumtibus erogatis, quatuor florenis; 2. Ernesti Clavim Ciceronianam, thalero; 3. Ciceronis Epistolas ad Atticum decem crucigeris; 4. Theophronem Campei, vernaculo idiomate, viginti et sex crucigeris; 5. Homei artem criticam, ex Anglica traductam in vernaculam a Meinhardo, floreno et quadraginta et quinque crucigeris; 6. Senecae opera philosophica crucigeris quindecim.

[Latin] The 3rd day before the Ides of December. My little library too has meanwhile been increased by some books. For I bought some time ago: 1. Livy, from my own treasury, at the expense of four florins; 2. Ernesti’s Ciceronian Key [Clavis Ciceroniana], for a thaler; 3. Cicero’s Letters to Atticus, for ten kreuzer; 4. Campe’s Theophron, in the vernacular, for twenty-six kreuzer; 5. Home’s art of criticism, translated from English into the vernacular by Meinhard, for one florin and forty-five kreuzer; 6. Seneca’s philosophical works for fifteen kreuzer.

Pridie Id. Debr. Quaestio hodie cum orta esset inter nos, praestare repetitio praeparationi aut haec illi, meum semper judicium fuit, optime utramvis jungi. Si vero defuerit altera alteri, equidem praeferendam esse repetitionem praeparationi. Intelligimus enim praeparati rem, ut ita dicam, dimidiam, nec vel totum haurimus sensum vel sinistrum. Edocti vero praeceptore et integrum, justum genuinumque sensum percipimus, qui repetitus menti sempiternus fere inducitur. Sed praeparati falsa verborum vi accepta, quae explanavit doctor, non diu, nisi repetatur, haeret et mox evanescit. Nobilibus hodie praesentibus Stuttgardiae peregrinis, publica musica vocum, nervorum cornuumque cantibus instituta est.

[Latin] The day before the Ides of December. A question having arisen today among us, whether repetition is better than preparation or the latter than the former, my judgment has always been that it is best for either to be joined with the other. If, however, one of the two should be lacking to the other, I for my part would hold that repetition should be preferred to preparation. For when we have prepared, we understand the matter, so to speak, only by half, and we draw out either not the whole sense or a perverse one. But when taught by the preceptor, we perceive the whole, just and genuine sense, which, repeated, is implanted in the mind almost for ever. But when we have prepared, the force of the words having been taken falsely, what the teacher has explained does not stick long unless it is repeated, and soon vanishes. Noble visitors being present today at Stuttgart, public music of voices, strings and horns was arranged.

Ipsis Id. Debr. Sollemnis hodie celebrata est et morum et studiorum VI classis auditorum perlustratio, quam vocant percursum, Durchgang. Hesterno die VII classis inquirebatur.

[Latin] On the Ides of December itself. Today the solemn inspection of the morals and studies of the auditors of the sixth class was held, which they call percursum, Durchgang [passage]. Yesterday the seventh class was being examined.

p. 441

XIX Cal. Jan. Nundinae annuae heri inchoatae, quibus res donandae natis festo die, quo Christi nativitas in memoriam revocatur, venum prostant. Heri praesertim, quo die e rure homines frequentissime adsunt, videres vino titubantes per vias bacchari, quorum unusquisque calceos aut alia vel sibi vel uxori vel natis emerat; videres [p. 441] innumeros hic lites agitari, illis merces licitari et alia multa. - Feriae nobis erant duobus his diebus, quorum primo dimidio negotia faciundo, reliquo tempore otia, jocos, discursitationes et ambulationes celebravi. Incumbit jam in me onus, fausta cuivis professorum precandi Jani Calendis, cui quidem negotio veteres praesertim medii aevi Latini poetae egregium praestant et praestiterunt auxilium.

[Latin] The 19th day before the Calends of January. The annual fair began yesterday, at which things to be given to children on the festal day on which the nativity of Christ is recalled are offered for sale. Yesterday especially, the day on which men from the country are present in greatest numbers, you could see them reeling with wine and revelling through the streets, each of whom had bought shoes or other things either for himself or for his wife or for his children; you could see [p. 441] countless disputes being waged here, wares being haggled over there, and many other things. — We had a holiday on these two days, of which I spent the first half in transacting business, the remaining time I devoted to leisure, jests, running about and walks. The burden now lies upon me of praying auspicious things for each of the professors on the Calends of Janus, in which task the old Latin poets, especially of the Middle Ages, provide and have provided excellent help.

XVIII Cal. Jan. Per semestre hoc hibernum placet jam, doctore et fautore maxime venerando Domino Hopfio praesertim suasore, Latina sumere et in his praecipue elaborare. Vacillor autem et in varias partes trahor, quo potissimum classico auctore uterer? Occurrerunt Ciceronis quaestiones Tusculanae, quas et Germanas facere et illustrare institui. Sed quae juvenilis est inconstantia, displicet jam consilium, si minus per Latinitatis obscuritatem et difficultatem, quae abest longissime ab hoc opere, per philosophiam et eloquentiam, quas potissimum, ut ipse ait, hic adhibere visum est.

[Latin] The 18th day before the Calends of January. For this winter semester I am pleased now, with my most venerable teacher and patron Herr Hopf especially as adviser, to take up Latin things and to work on these especially. But I vacillate and am drawn in various directions as to which classical author I should use above all. There occurred to me Cicero’s Tusculan Questions, which I resolved both to make German and to illustrate. But, such is juvenile inconstancy, my plan now displeases me, if less on account of the obscurity and difficulty of the Latinity, which is very far from this work, than on account of philosophy and eloquence, which, as he himself says, it seemed best to employ here.

XVII Cal. Jan. Nox erat et tranquilla mente libello cuidam obsidebam, cum flagrare in urbe nostra aedem sonitus campanae nos exterreret. Heu, quantus omnes invasit metus! Invalescente jam incendio, ego meusque pater auxilium ivimus domui cuidam vicinitatis. Ibi vero videres aedem flagrantem totam igne et paene jam incendio consumtam. Domum illam cum pervenissemus, senescere jam coepit flamma et paullo post evanescere paene et fumum late tolli ad astra. Quid plura? Hora vix elapsa restincta est flamma, consumta domus dimidia.

[Latin] The 17th day before the Calends of January. It was night and, with a tranquil mind, I was sitting over a certain little book when the sound of bells, that a house in our city was burning, terrified us. Alas, what fear seized all! As the fire was already gaining strength, I and my father went to the aid of a certain house in the neighborhood. There you could see the house blazing all over with fire and almost already consumed by the conflagration. When we had come to that house, the flame began to die down and a little later almost to vanish, and the smoke to be borne far up to the stars. What more? Scarcely an hour had passed when the flame was extinguished, half the house consumed.

XVI Cal. Jan. Causam vero, quae incendium commoverit, sexcenties variant. Narrant plerique, plumbo, quod ajunt, infuso. Sed et hic differunt alii. Quid tamen recensio tot rumorum proficiat?. Consentiunt vero plerique, filiae Praeceptoris ineptias nugasque et aetate et ordine indignissimas igni fuisse causam, quae quidem, dum salvare vellet lectum aliquem, valde et cripes et faciem et vestimenta cremata est.

[Latin] The 16th day before the Calends of January. The cause, however, which started the fire, they vary six hundred times. Most narrate that it was lead, as they say, poured in. But here too others differ. Yet what would the review of so many rumors accomplish? Most agree, however, that the follies and trifles of the preceptor’s daughter, most unworthy of her age and station, were the cause of the fire; who, while she wished to save a certain bed, was badly burned in hair, face and clothing.

XII Cal. Jan. Bruma fuit hodie et dies S. Thomae festus. Jam jam gravissimum anni tempus cum sustinuerimus, id certe solatur, quod nunc dies in posterum magis magisque augeantur. Parvus etiam institutus est in nostra domo vocum nervorumque concentus, quo Dominus Oberst de Rau, inhabitans superiorem nostrae aedis partem, adfuit, quo digrediente venit Dom. Secret. Moser eiusque uxor, Dom. Secret. Günzler eiusdemque uxor et Dom. Zoror, frater duarum uxorum.

[Latin] The 12th day before the Calends of January. It was the winter solstice today and the feast day of St. Thomas. Now that we have borne the heaviest time of the year, this at least consoles, that now the days will be increased more and more in future. A small concert of voices and strings was also arranged in our house, at which Colonel de Rau, who lives in the upper part of our house, was present; when he departed there came Secretary Moser and his wife, Secretary Günzler and his wife, and Herr Zoror, brother of the two wives.

p. 442

XI Cal. Jan. Jam dudum equidem antea, quam gravi morbo implicarer, quae consequuta sunt et mala et bona perturbationum animi, explicare pro mei ingenii modulo incepi. Quae honoris, jam exposui. Multa quoque bona sequuta esse, nemo negaverit, si homini, qui captus ea libidine fuit, quaesivit honorem ex bene factis. Ubiquidem facta rectissima, consilia vero, si per honorem capta sint, minus probe dixeris. Recte enim facta, ubi virtute perpetrentur, non lucri sui cupidine, ea maxime sunt laudanda.

[Latin] The 11th day before the Calends of January. Long since, indeed, before I was entangled in a grave illness, I began, so far as my modest talent allows, to explain the evils and goods that followed from the perturbations of the mind. Those of honor I have already set out. That many good things too followed, no one will deny, if the man who was seized by that desire sought honor from good deeds. Wherever indeed the deeds are most upright, the plans, however, if adopted through honor, you would call less upright. For right deeds, when they are accomplished from virtue, not from desire for one’s own gain, are most of all to be praised.

X Cal. Jan. Ordiamur jam auri opumque libidinem, quae sive sordida avaritia est, sive dehonestans pecuniae injuria quaerendae cupido. Quod si prior, quam dixi, avaritia, occupaverit animum, aliis minus, quam sibi ipse nocet. Hominum est infelicissimus etc. Die Schilderung schließt endlich mit der Bemerkung, daß der Geizige auch gegen seine Familie und Diener treulos, grausam sein müsse; maxima tamen fraus, si principis fuerit minister, in dominum, cui fidum esse vel juramento se obstrinxit.

[Latin] The 10th day before the Calends of January. Let us now begin with the desire for gold and wealth, which is either sordid avarice or a dishonoring desire of acquiring money by injustice. But if the former, which I have called avarice, has taken hold of the mind, it harms others less than himself. He is the most unhappy of men, etc. The description concludes finally with the remark that the miser must also be faithless and cruel toward his own family and servants; [Latin] yet the greatest fraud, if he is a prince’s minister, is against the master to whom he has bound himself even by oath to be faithful.

VIII Cal. Jan. Die Solis. Dies hodie beatissimo nostro servatori festus obortus est, ubi ex more et ego lautissimis a patre muneribus sum affectus, quorum quidem cum sint multa gratissima, jucundissimum tamen utilissimumque est Schelleri Lexicon, cujus praestantiam usu saepius ipse jam percepi.

[Latin] The 8th day before the Calends of January. Sunday. A day festal for our most blessed Savior has arisen today, on which, as is the custom, I too was favored by my father with most splendid gifts; of which, although many are most welcome, the most pleasant and useful is Scheller’s Lexicon, whose excellence I have already myself often perceived by use.

Ipsis Cal. Jan. 1786. Novus igitur sub DEI auspiciis annus inluxit. Mediis his diebus emi mihi etiam Schelleri praecepta styli bene Latini imprimis Ciceroniani.

[Latin] On the Calends of January itself, 1786. The new year has thus dawned under the auspices of GOD. In the midst of these days I bought for myself also Scheller’s precepts of good Latin style, above all the Ciceronian.

III Id. Febr. 1786. Redeamus jam ad prisca haec nostra stylo exercendo instituta, intermissa longo intervallo temporis, cum sit hodie Serenissimi Domini nostri Ducis natalis LIXtus Nescio quo casu concionem, qua explicabatur Cap. IX Sapientiae Salomonis, nullam adivi. Post meridiem audivi orationem in Gymnasio Dom. Prof. Schmidtii, quae egit de meritis nostri Ducis de re litteraria Wirtembergiue et quidem exposuit excellentia, quae de Tubingensi studiorum Universitate demeritus erat; deinde, quae de nostro Gymnasio, postea de scholis claustralibus; sequebantur scholae triviales et quas vocant Germanae; excepit has splendida institutio Academiae primo quidem militaris, insequenti tempore complexu hujus instituti amplificato, et literariae; addidit denique et institutum sexui sequiori consulendo, quam vocant scholam, école. Clausit totam orationem ardentibus pro salute Ducis nostri eiusque maritae nunc peregrinantium votis precibusque.

[Latin] The 3rd day before the Ides of February, 1786. Let us now return to these our earlier exercises for practicing style, interrupted for a long interval of time, since today is the fifty-ninth birthday of our Most Serene Lord the Duke. By what chance I know not, I attended no sermon in which Chapter IX of the Wisdom of Solomon was expounded. In the afternoon I heard in the Gymnasium an oration of Professor Schmidt, which dealt with the merits of our Duke toward literary affairs of Württemberg and indeed expounded the excellences in which he had deserved well of the University of Tübingen; then those toward our Gymnasium, afterwards toward the cloister schools; there followed the trivial schools and those they call German ones; these were succeeded by the splendid institution of the Academy, at first indeed military, afterwards, the scope of this institution having been enlarged, also literary; he added finally also an institution for providing for the weaker sex, which they call a school, école. He closed the whole oration with ardent vows and prayers for the welfare of our Duke and his consort, now traveling.

p. 443

Obschon Hegel mit dieser Uebersicht aller damaligen Bildungsanstalten Würtembergs einen neuen Anlauf nahm, seinen Lateinischen Styl durch den Anreiz eines Tagebuchs unaufhörlich zu üben und zu verbessern, so muß es ihm doch entweder an erregsamem Stoff zu Aufzeichnungen gefehlt oder sein Eifer durch hinreichenden Erfolg sich befriedigt gesehen haben. Es kommen von jekt ab nur noch einige allgemeinere Betrachtungen in Lateinischer Sprache vor. Die eine derselben aus dem März 1786 enthält das Brouillon zu einer Lateinischen Rede über die Geselligkeit, welche er auf dem Gymnasium im Lauf des Sommers halten wollte, wenn die Reihe solcher rhetorischen Uebung an ihn käme. Er legt es dabei darauf an, in der Anordnung so schulgerecht als möglich zu Werke zu gehen und in der Ausführung alle traditionellen Schmuckphrasen und für Ciceronianisch gehaltenen Uebergangswendungen anzubringen. Es würde ermüdend sein, das Ganze mitzutheilen; einige Puncte jedoch, über den Vortheil, welchen der Umgang mit älteren Personen darbietet, über die Nothwendigkeit der Beobachtung der geselligen Formen, über die Grenzen der Geselligkeit und über den Umgang mit dem schwächeren Geschlecht sind zu charakteristisch für Hegel selbst, als daß sie nicht ausgehoben zu werden verdienten. Uebrigens ist das Latein wirklich nur Brouillonlatein:

Although Hegel, with this survey of all the educational institutions then existing in Württemberg, made a new start at practicing and improving his Latin style incessantly through the stimulus of a diary, he must nevertheless either have lacked stimulating material for entries or have seen his zeal satisfied by adequate success. From now on there occur only a few more general reflections in the Latin language. One of them, from March 1786, contains the rough draft of a Latin speech on sociability, which he wished to deliver at the Gymnasium in the course of the summer, when the turn for such rhetorical exercise should come to him. He aims thereby to proceed as scholastically correct as possible in the arrangement and to bring in, in the execution, all the traditional ornamental phrases and transitional turns held to be Ciceronian. It would be tiresome to communicate the whole; but some points, on the advantage which association with older persons offers, on the necessity of observing the social forms, on the limits of sociability and on association with the weaker sex, are too characteristic of Hegel himself for them not to deserve being extracted. Moreover the Latin is really only rough-draft Latin:

p. 444

„Primum ergo et potissimum cum natu majoribus conversatis redundat commodum, quod multas rerum multarum notitias sibi comparent. Accedit imprimis notitia, quae nulli vel aliquo cum fructu in aliorum salute laboranti, vel se ipse non velit riteorbi committere cum summo detrimento, haec est notitia hominum. Addamus, qua re in nostris temporibus moribusque praesertim supersederi nequit, ritus quosdam et externa specie formaque se commendandi facillime discet, qui versatus fuerit diu in hominibus politis cultisque et moribus; ut ita dicam, longa cum mundo consuetudine tritus. Cum, qui ab externa parte non nitet, et eadem animi stupiditate laborare creditur. Cum tanta igitur fluant e consuetudine justa cum aliis hominibus, necesse est, ex perversa et nimi, si ita dicere fas est, multa scaturire mala. Quae sunt: a. animi dissipatio et distractio; b. amissio temporis; c. alienatio etfastidium ab omni re, severiorem animum poscente et ab solitudine. Venio jam ad consuetudinem sexus sequioris, quo quidem scopulo multi et praeclarissimi animo misere perierunt. Quid ergo faciendum? Abstinendum omni plane cum illis commercio? Nati sumus, ut dixi, ea lege, qui commercium et consuetudinem colamus. At feminae non sunt homines? Quis hoc contendet? Utendum igitur est illis. Sed quaeritur, quae et quantae ca [p. 444] lamitates consequantur? Caret consuetudo illa omnibus commodis? Absit! Immo, si recte utaris, maxima tibi offeret. Qui enim, quod sane quisque Vestrûm et volet et velit, hos inter homines, qui nunc globum tuentur, fortunatus cupit esse, eum abjicere necesse est, ut ita dicam: Schlacken, quod nusquam melius et diligentius fieri poterit, quam in societate illarum. Habent enim laudisque infamiaeque monopolium! "

“[Latin] First, then, and foremost, there accrues to those who converse with their elders the advantage that they procure for themselves the knowledge of many things. To this is added, above all, a knowledge which no one, whether he labors with some fruit for the welfare of others or does not wish to commit himself properly to the world, [can lack] without the greatest detriment — this is the knowledge of men. Let us add — a thing which in our times and customs especially cannot be dispensed with — that he will most easily learn certain rites and the art of commending oneself by outward appearance and form who has long been versed among polished and cultivated men and manners; worn, so to speak, by long familiarity with the world. For he who does not shine on the outward side is believed to labor under the same dullness of mind. — Since, then, so many benefits flow from just intercourse with other men, it is necessary that from a perverse and excessive [intercourse], if one may so say, many evils spring forth. These are: a. dissipation and distraction of the mind; b. loss of time; c. alienation and distaste for everything that requires a more serious mind, and for solitude. — I come now to the intercourse of the weaker sex, a reef on which many, and the most distinguished in spirit, have miserably perished. What then is to be done? Must one abstain wholly from any commerce with them? We are born, as I said, under the law that we cultivate commerce and intercourse. But are women not human beings? Who will contend this? We must therefore use them. But it is asked what and how great calamities [p. 444] follow? Is that intercourse devoid of all advantages? Far from it! On the contrary, if you use it rightly, it will offer you the greatest. For he who, as surely each of you both wants and would want, desires to be fortunate among the men who now inhabit the globe, must cast off, so to speak: Schlacken [dross], which nowhere can be done better and more diligently than in the society of these women. For they have the monopoly of praise and of infamy!”

Eine wichtige Reflexion enthält eine andere Stelle des Tagebuchs aus demselben Monat. Hegel vergleicht darin die Religion des Ethnicismus mit dem gewöhnlichen christlichen Glauben. Da die Schriftsteller der Alten eine so reiche Quelle intellectueller und sittlicher Bildung für ihn waren, so stieß er sich an der wegwerfenden Weise, mit welcher Viele die Alten ihrer Religion wegen behandelten. Er fand aus, daß, was man ihnen als Aberglauben zurechne, denen selbst nicht fremd sei, welche solche Vorwürfe machten. Er überzeugte sich, daß der Glaube an Engel und Teufel nur eine Wiederholung des antiken Dämonenglaubens sei. Er verabscheute die Consequenzen, welche aus einer solchen Vorstellung für die Freiheit des Menschen sich ergeben müssen. Er erkannte die göttliche Würde des Menschen darin, daß er für seine guten und bösen Thaten selbst verantwortlich sei.

An important reflection is contained in another passage of the diary from the same month. Hegel compares therein the religion of heathenism with the ordinary Christian faith. Since the writers of the ancients were such a rich source of intellectual and ethical culture for him, he took offense at the disparaging manner in which many treated the ancients on account of their religion. He found that what is charged against them as superstition is not alien to those themselves who made such reproaches. He convinced himself that the belief in angels and devils is only a repetition of the antique belief in demons. He abhorred the consequences which must result from such a representation for the freedom of man. He recognized the divine dignity of man in this, that he is himself responsible for his good and evil deeds.

p. 445

V Id. Martii 1786. Saepe mihi de collustratis nostris temporibus cogitanti incurrit et in animum, saepe a nobis convicia et illusiones jaci in varios errores paganorum et omnino in omnium priscorum mores et vetustate firmatas opiniones. Quae nunc de illis recurrent menti, paucis calamo mandabo. In explicanda Deûm historia universaque mythologia audivi, cum illuderetur priscis, de superstitione ipsorum, quippe qui duos sibi praeesse credebant genios, alterum bonum, alterum malum, hos perpetua concertatione congredi, quorum si bonus malum superaret, bene ab homine et cogitari et agi; si contra vinceret malus hominemque dominaretur, prava et menti occurrere et in prave acta erumpere hominem. Deliberans, an eadem nostri aevi tenerentur opinione, inveni, plurimos omnia bene cogitata et facta divinis viribus, prave viribus diaboli adsignare. Parum differre inter se has utriusque aevi opiniones quisque viderit. Accedit quamvis unus diabolus toti generi humano, unicuique et singulo insidiari semper dicatur, id tamen auget similitudinem, quod unus homo probus unum pluresve habere angelos, vitae suae morumque custodes, qui recedant ab hominibus pravis, creditur. Si quis forsan homo ex plebe commisit aliquid contra leges, hoc suam culpam diluere aliqua ex parte putant, quod Deum dicant ab ipso cessisse passumque esse, ut cade [p. 445] ret. At id est divinae bonitatis providentia. Est quidem, at repugnaret consilio, quo homines formavit. Voluit enim non deficere aliquod in rerum universi catena membrum, quod esset inter bestias, quo ferreis instincti vinculis coacti, libertate carentes, bonum an malum eligant, suo nihil consilio faciunt, et inter aethereum illud angelorum genus, qui ab omni malo alieni nonnisi recta perficiunt. Relictus est igitur homini medius inter hos locus, cujus plane arbitrio datum, utrum bonum an malum eligat.

[Latin] The 5th day before the Ides of March, 1786. Often, as I think about our enlightened times, it also occurs to my mind that reproaches and mockeries are often hurled by us against the various errors of the pagans and in general against the customs of all the ancients and the opinions confirmed by antiquity. What now recurs to my mind concerning them I shall commit to the pen in a few words. In the explanation of the history of the Gods and of mythology as a whole I heard, when the ancients were being mocked, about their superstition, since they believed that two genii presided over them, one good, the other evil; that these meet in perpetual conflict; and that if the good overcame the evil, things are well thought and done by man; if on the contrary the evil conquered and dominated man, depraved things both occur to the mind and the man breaks forth into wickedly done acts. Deliberating whether the opinion of our own age were the same, I found that very many assign all things well thought and done to divine powers, wickedly done to the powers of the devil. Everyone will see that these opinions of the two ages differ little from one another. Add that, although one devil is said always to lie in wait for the whole human race and for each single one, yet this increases the similarity, that one upright man is believed to have one or more angels, guardians of his life and morals, who withdraw from wicked men. If perchance some man of the common people has committed something against the laws, they think to wash away his guilt in some part by this, that they say God withdrew from him and permitted that he should fall, [p. 445] But that is the providence of divine goodness. It is indeed, but it would conflict with the design by which He formed men. For He willed that there should not be lacking in the chain of the universe of things a certain link, which should stand between the beasts — who, compelled by the iron bonds of instinct and lacking the liberty [to decide] whether they choose good or evil, do nothing by their own counsel — and that ethereal race of angels, who, alien to all evil, accomplish only what is right. There was left therefore to man the middle place between these, to whose entire discretion it is given whether he choose good or evil.

Simili errore multos e Christianis irridere vidi. Crediderunt quippe pagani pacari Deûm iras jejuniis, cibis potuque Deo appositis. Referamus id ad nostra tempora. Multis in ritibus eandem adhuc durare superstitionem vidi, ut in sepulchralibus aliisque apud collustratiores Lutheranos. Ast apud Catholicos totus ad hanc diem viget. Hoc solo differunt. Pagani apposuere ipsis Diis cibos suos; quos si sacerdotes devoraverint, a Diis esse comestos putaverunt. Hodie non item. Superstitiosi enim hi homunciones pecuniam, alimenta atque alia tradunt sacerdotibus eoque gratiam Dei aucupant. Sed quae major, quae horribilior superstitio stultitia fuit?

I have seen many of the Christians deride a like error. For the pagans believed that the wrath of the Gods is appeased by fasts, and by food and drink set before God. Let us refer this to our own times. In many rites I have seen the same superstition still persist, as in funeral rites and others among the more enlightened Lutherans. But among the Catholics it flourishes entire to this day. In this alone they differ. The pagans set their own foods before the Gods themselves; if the priests devoured them, they thought they had been eaten by the Gods. Today it is not so. For these superstitious little men hand over money, victuals and other things to the priests and thereby hunt after the favor of God. But what greater, what more horrible superstition or folly has there been?

Am 18. März folgt eine moralische Betrachtung über den Zorn, welchen Hegel auch in Ansehung von Schandthaten nicht zugeben will: non necesse est, in iram abripi; satis est, dolere de sceleribus aegreque ea ferre. Endlich am 22. März schließt er: si quis tam adeo sibi imperare didicit -, ut nulla re in iram moveatur, ei liceat, succensere sceleribus! Unmittelbar darauf schreibt er: „Alle Menschen haben die Absicht, sich glücklich zu machen, mit einigen seltenen Ausnahmen, die, um Andere glücklich zu machen, so viel Erhabenheit der Seele besaßen, sich aufzuopfern. Doch diese haben, glaub ' ich, nicht wahre Glückseligkeit aufgeopfert, sondern nur zeitliche Vortheile, zeitliches Glück, auch Leben. Diese machen also hier noch keine Ausnahme. "

On 18 March there follows a moral reflection on anger, which Hegel does not wish to admit even in regard to infamous deeds: [Latin] it is not necessary to be carried away into anger; it is enough to grieve over crimes and to bear them with distress. Finally on 22 March he concludes: [Latin] if anyone has learned so far to command himself that he is moved to anger by nothing, let him be permitted to be angry at crimes! — Immediately afterward he writes: “All human beings have the intention of making themselves happy, with a few rare exceptions who, in order to make others happy, possessed so much sublimity of soul as to sacrifice themselves. Yet these, I believe, have not sacrificed true blessedness, but only temporal advantages, temporal happiness, also life. These therefore make no exception here.” —

Dann folgt noch ohne Anfang und Ende ein Fragment über die Aufklärung durch Wissenschaft und Kunst, aus welchem folgende Bemerkungen nicht übergangen werden dürfen: „Einen Entwurf von einer Aufklärung des gemeinen Mannes zu machen, halte ich theils für die meisten auch gelehrtesten Leute sehr schwer, theils aber auch besonders für mich viel schwerer, da ich überhaupt die Geschichte noch nicht philosophisch und gründlich studirt habe. Sonst glaube ich auch, diese Aufklärung des gemeinen Mannes habe sich immer nach der Religion seiner Zeit gerichtet. -- In Ansehung der Wissenschaften und Künste bin ich also der Meinung, sie haben zuerst im Orient geblüht und seien dann von da aus immer mehr nach Westen gewandert.

Then there follows, without beginning and end, a fragment on enlightenment through science and art, from which the following remarks must not be passed over: “To make a draft of an enlightenment of the common man I hold partly for most, even the most learned people, very difficult, partly however also especially for me much harder, since I have in general not yet studied history philosophically and thoroughly. Otherwise I believe that this enlightenment of the common man has always oriented itself according to the religion of its time. — With regard to the sciences and arts I am therefore of the opinion that they flourished first in the Orient and then migrated from there more and more toward the West.

p. 446

So sehr man nun heut zu Tage, wenigstens in Betreff der Philosophie, das große Rühmen von der Gelehrsamkeit der Aegyptier mit Recht vermeidet, so bleibt doch so viel gewiß, daß sie es wenigstens in Ansehung der mechanischen und bildenden Künste zu einem solchen Grad der Vollkommenheit gebracht haben, daß noch jest die Trümmer ihrer Kunstwerke bewundert werden, und es ist sehr wahrscheinlich, daß die großen und weitläuftigen praktischen - Kenntnisse auch schon in eine genauere Theorie gebracht worden seien. "

Much as one nowadays, at least in respect of philosophy, rightly avoids the great praise of the learning of the Egyptians, so much at least remains certain, that in regard to the mechanical and the fine arts they brought themselves to such a degree of perfection that even now the ruins of their works of art are admired; and it is very probable that the great and extensive practical knowledge had also already been brought into a more exact theory.” —

Weiter findet sich nichts aus dem Jahre 1786. Mit den ersten Tagen des nächsten Jahres sekt er noch einmal zu einem Tagebuch an, hält es aber nur eine Woche lang aus. Um so nothwendiger wird die Mittheilung dieser Selbstschilderung sein. Eine noch entschiedenere Selbstständigkeit, etwa abgerechnet, findet sich im Wesen keine Veränderung. Es ist immer das Streben nach wissenschaftlicher Ausbildung im Vordergrunde; daneben ergreift die Reflexion aber auch, was von dem allgemeinen Leben sich Interessantes darbietet; an sich selbst denkt er am wenigsten. Seine einzige durchgreifende Eigenheit ist die Selbstlosigkeit der objectivsten Sinnesart.

Nothing further is found from the year 1786. With the first days of the next year he sets about a diary once more, but keeps it up for only a week. All the more necessary will be the communication of this self-portrayal. Apart perhaps from a still more decided independence, no change is to be found in his nature. The striving for scientific cultivation is always in the foreground; alongside it, however, reflection also seizes upon whatever of interest the general life presents; of himself he thinks least. His one pervasive peculiarity is the selflessness of the most objective cast of mind.

p. 447

Am 1. Januar 1787. Gegenwärtig bin ich das erste Jahr in der siebenten Classe des hiesigen Gymnasiums. Mein Hauptaugenmerk sind noch immer die Sprachen und zwar wirklich die Griechische und Lateinische. Daneben arbeite ich zuweilen etwas in der Mathematik. Außer den öffentlichen Lectionen höre ich ein Collegium bei Herrn Prof. Hopf, worin wir 3 Stunden dem Longin und eine Stunde den Pflichten des Cicero widmen. Von der Art, wie wir sie lesen, ist unnöthig, etwas zu sagen. Einige Zeit wende ich auch auf Ausarbeitung kleiner Aufsäße und Niederschreibung meiner Gedanken. Sonntags arbeite ich meist in der sphärischen Trigonometrie und zum Theil widme ich ihn guten Freunden. Uebrige Viertelstunden fülle ich wirklich mit Lesung und Excerpirung der Excurse Heyne's zu seinem Virgil aus. Den Vormittag fing ich an, in der sphärischen Trigonometrie, die ich aus Lorenzen's Mathematik abgeschrieben hatte, etwas durchzugehen. Allein ich wurde durch Visiten, die zu Neujahr Glück wünschten, bald unterbrochen und nachher mußte ich in gleichen Angelegenheiten ausgehen. Den Nachmittag wollte ich nur Einiges in Sophiens Reise lesen, ich konnte mich aber nimmer davon losreißen bis an den Abend, wo ich in das Concert ging. Es ist nämlich gewöhnlich, daß alle Neujahr Deputirte von Eflingen dem Herzog unter dem Titel Schusgeld 100 Ducaten überreichen, worauf denn allemal in der Akademie ein Concert veranstaltet wird. Von diesem konnte man zwar we [p. 447] gen dem Getose der vielen Zuhörer wenig hören, allein die Zeit wurde mir doch sehr angenehm verkürzt, indem ich da gute Freunde sprach, die ich schon lange nimmer gesehen hatte. Das Anschauen schöner Mädchen trug zu unserer Unterhaltung auch nicht wenig bei.

On 1 January 1787. At present I am in the first year in the seventh class of the local Gymnasium. My chief concerns are still the languages, and indeed really Greek and Latin. Besides that I work now and then a little in mathematics. Apart from the public lessons I attend a lecture course with Professor Hopf, in which we devote 3 hours to Longinus and one hour to the Duties of Cicero. Of the manner in which we read them it is unnecessary to say anything. Some time I also give to the working out of small essays and to writing down my thoughts. On Sundays I work mostly at spherical trigonometry, and in part I devote them to good friends. Remaining quarter-hours I really fill out with reading and excerpting Heyne’s excursuses to his Virgil. In the forenoon I began to go through a little of the spherical trigonometry that I had copied out of Lorentzen’s Mathematics. But I was soon interrupted by visits that came to wish a happy New Year, and afterwards I had to go out on like errands. In the afternoon I meant only to read a little in Sophie’s Journey, but I could never tear myself away from it until the evening, when I went to the concert. For it is the custom that every New Year deputies from Esslingen present the Duke, under the title of protection money, with 100 ducats, whereupon each time a concert is arranged in the Academy. Of this one could, to be sure, hear little because of [p. 447] the din of the many listeners, but the time was nevertheless made very pleasantly short for me by my speaking there with good friends whom I had not seen for a long time. The sight of beautiful girls also contributed not a little to our conversation.

Dienstag den 2. Januar. Gewöhnlich; ich excerpirte Abends aus Heyne's Ercursen.

Tuesday, the 2nd of January. As usual; in the evening I excerpted from Heyne’s excursuses.

Mittwoch den 3. Ianuar. Es war diese Nacht eine totale Mondfinsterniß. Herr Prof. Hopf rüstete auf dem Gymnasio einige Sehrohre zur Beobachtung aus dem neuen Apparat der Instrumente. Es kamen Einige, aber der ganz überzogene Himmel ließ nicht das Mindeste sehen. Herr Rector, illuminirt, erzählte uns unter Anderem: er sei auch als Gymnasiast mit Andern Observator gewesen und des Nachts stellatum gegangen. Sie seien aber nur herumvagirt. Es kamen Stadtphilister dazu, die sie einziehen wollten. Die Gymnasiasten sagten: sie seien stellatum gegangen. Ei, sagten die Soldaten, sie sollten bei Nacht in ihren Betten liegen und bei Tag stellatum gehen.

Wednesday, the 3rd of January. This night there was a total lunar eclipse. Professor Hopf equipped some telescopes at the Gymnasium for observation, from the new apparatus of instruments.
